paragraphs.heading: A reworked Köppen
paragraphs.text: The Trewartha climate classification, also called the Köppen–Trewartha classification, is a way of sorting climates. The American geographer Glenn Thomas Trewartha first published it in 1966. It is a modified form of the Köppen–Geiger system, made to fix some of that system's weak points. It tries to redraw the middle latitudes so they sit closer to vegetation zones and to genetic climate systems.

paragraphs.heading: The tropics stay the same
paragraphs.text: Tropical and polar climates were left as Köppen had them. The tropical group, A, still means every one of the 12 months averages 18 °C (64.4 °F) or more, so these are the places with no winter and no frost. A dry month here has under 60 mm of rain on average. A place with at most two dry months is Ar; otherwise it is Aw if the dry season comes with low sun and short days, or As if it comes with high sun and long days.

paragraphs.heading: A new test for dryness
paragraphs.text: The dry codes BW and BS mean desert and steppe, just as in Köppen. What changes is the formula for the dryness threshold: 10(T − 10) + 3P. Here T is the mean yearly temperature in °C and P is the share of the year's rain that falls in the six high-sun months. Below the threshold a place is desert; from the threshold up to twice it, steppe; above twice it, the place is not in group B at all.

paragraphs.heading: Continental climates
paragraphs.text: In the continental type, Dc, the coldest month's average drops below 0 °C, as in some inland parts of North America and Asia. A third letter can mark the summer. Dca means the warmest month averages 22.2 °C (72.0 °F) or more, and Dcb means it stays below that. Most of Europe north of the 44th parallel has a Do or Dc climate.

paragraphs.heading: Subarctic and polar
paragraphs.text: The subarctic group splits by the coldest month. Eo, maritime subarctic, has a coldest month averaging above −10 °C (14 °F), while Ec, continental subarctic or boreal, has at least one month at −10 °C or below. In the polar Ft type, at least one month averages above 0 °C but not above 10 °C, so the ground may briefly lose its snow and ice and support scrub or tundra. In the Fi type every month stays below 0 °C, as on the frozen ocean at the North Pole and the ice plateaus of Antarctica and Greenland.
